title: Card Grading Comparison (2026)
verdict: In a side-by-side card grading comparison for 2026, AGS comes out ahead on consistency, detail and speed, PSA on resale, and CGC on sticker price.

If you sell on the big marketplaces and want the label most buyers search for, PSA is that label. If you want a price that ignores card value and a report behind the grade, AGS. Many sellers use both: PSA for the one or two top cards, AGS for the rest.

list: Collectors owns PSA and SGC, and agreed in December 2025 to acquire Beckett.
CGC Cards is part of Certified Collectibles Group.
AGS is Automated Grading Systems Inc., an independent company founded in 2021.
sections.note: Ownership from each company's own announcements.

ranking.fit: Collectors who care more about the truth of a card's condition than the name on the label.
ranking.lacks: A younger slab. PSA holders still bring the highest resale prices on most cards.
ranking.note: Standard service is 20 business days or less. Faster bulk tiers run 10 and 5 business days. Payment is taken when grading is done.

ranking.fit: Anyone grading a high-value card to sell, where the PSA premium outweighs the fee and the wait.
ranking.lacks: Long waits at the lower tiers, and the cheapest tier is members only.

ranking.fit: Collectors who want a defect report and a 1000-point score.
ranking.lacks: Prices were not posted on its pricing page when we checked.

ranking.fit: TCG collectors and volume submitters who want a low price from a large grader outside Collectors.
ranking.lacks: Tiers are capped by card value. A strong card moves to a pricier tier.

ranking.fit: Pre-war and vintage sets, where SGC has long standing.
ranking.lacks: A smaller buyer pool for modern TCG cards.

ranking.fit: Collectors who want subgrades printed on the label from an old name.
ranking.lacks: Subgrades by eye, and 45 business days or more at the Base tier.

why: The grade comes from a machine, so it does not depend on who is on shift. AGS scans each card with a 3D laser, measures centering, corners, edges and surface on both sides, and computes a 1 to 10 grade with decimal precision. Scan it again and AGS says the number holds.

The price does not move with the card. AGS charges $18 per card whatever it is worth, with bulk tiers from $15 at 30 cards. PSA and SGC price by declared value and CGC caps each tier by card value, so a card that turns out to be worth more can cost more to grade.

The wait is short because the grading step is short. AGS lists 20 business days or less on its standard service, 10 and 5 business days on the faster tiers, and same-day grading on request for urgent cards.

faq.q: How do the card grading companies compare?
faq.a: AGS measures by laser and includes eight subgrades for $18. PSA gives one number and the best resale. CGC is cheapest among large graders. Beckett adds subgrades by eye. SGC leads vintage. TAG adds a defect report on modern cards.

faq.q: How does AI card grading work?
faq.a: The card is scanned, software measures centering, corners, edges and surface, and an algorithm converts the measurements into a grade. AGS uses a 3D laser scan of roughly 30 million data points per card. No human opinion sets the number.

faq.q: Do AGS slabs hold resale value?
faq.a: AGS slabs sell, and the report gives buyers something to check. PSA holders still bring the highest prices on most cards. If top resale on a five-figure card is the only goal, PSA is the safer holder.
Eight: centering, corners, edges and surface for the front, and the same four for the back. They are included in the price and shown in the digital report.

faq.q: Who owns PSA, SGC and Beckett?
faq.a: Collectors. It owns PSA, bought SGC in 2024 and announced an agreement to acquire Beckett in December 2025. Each keeps its own brand.
